title: Maghsoodloo Wins Star-Studded Freestyle Friday
summary: GM Parham Maghsoodloo took a step closer to qualifying for the 2027 FIDE Freestyle Chess World Championship by taking out the latest edition of Freestyle Friday. Maghsoodloo scored 9/11 en route to victory, suffering only a single loss to one of Uzbekistan's Olympiad heroes, GM Nodirbek Yakubboev, along the way. GM Oleksandr Bortnyk secured second place after winning his last three games, while IM Sergey Sklokin and GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda rounded out the top four. WGM Dina Belenkaya commentated live on YouTube while participating, which you can view here: An illustrious field of 112 masters participated in October's second Freestyle Friday, including no fewer than six current or former 2700 FIDE-rated players: Maghsoodloo, Yakubboev, Duda, GM Amin Tabatabaei, GM Gata Kamsky, and GM Vincent Keymer, graced the event with their presence. The former women's world champion and GM Alexandra Kosteniuk, two-time women's world blitz champion GM Anna Muzychuk, and several prominent content creators also played, including the aforementioned Belenkaya, WFM Anna Cramling, and GM Eric Hansen. Less than a day after winning the first 3 0 Thursday of the week, Duda emerged as a frontrunner after besting Keymer in round six. Their duel had all the hallmarks and complexity of a clash between two super-GMs and it was fitting that the game was decided in the throes of time trouble.

title: Between the Silk Road and the chessboard - eight days in Uzbekistan
summary:
Bukhara, Samarkand, Tashkent

The German-Dutch rivalry is legendary. Often, merely recalling it is enough for both sides to bring out stories that the other would probably tell rather differently.

In that sense, our travel group was a small European experiment: nine Dutch, five Germans and one Italian. From 21 to 29 September, we travelled through Uzbekistan – along the old Silk Road from Bukhara via Samarkand to Tashkent. The trip was organised and accompanied by Ardjan Langedijk, a chess player and owner of Central Asia Tours in Heemstede, a travel company specialising in Central Asia. We wanted to discover a country that was unfamiliar to most of us, get to know its people and culture and, of course, experience the Chess Olympiad.

The fact that Germany and the Netherlands faced each other twice in sporting contests during our trip added a nice touch. In football, the match ended peacefully at 1-1. In chess, things were ultimately a little less diplomatic.

Bukhara - like a film set

After the overnight flight via Istanbul, we landed in Bukhara in the morning. A little sleep had to suffice, and then we headed out. During our very first walk around the city, we had a feeling that would return again and again over the following days: is this really real - or are we walking through a film set?

The Kalon Mosque

Mosques and madrasas, sand-coloured walls and bright blue domes, narrow alleyways and small courtyards in between. We saw the roughly thousand-year-old Samanid Mausoleum, the imposing Kalon Mosque and, of course, Lyabi-Hauz, the square around the old pond, a place where one does not merely want to look around, but simply to stay.

There we also came across an old acquaintance - Nasreddin Hodja. From Turkey through the Balkans and Central Asia to India, stories are told of his tricks and wisdom. In Bukhara, he sits as a bronze figure on his donkey beside the Nadir Divan-Begi Madrasa and is one of the most photographed residents of the city.

Nasreddin Hodja

In the late afternoon, the courtyard of the madrasa was transformed into a catwalk. Music, traditional dances and a fashion show featuring colourful Uzbek garments against the historic backdrop – our welcome to Uzbekistan could hardly have been more impressive.

Musical accompaniment to the fashion show

But we were not only cultural tourists. We are also chess players.

Chess match at Lyabi-Hauz Square

Peter, right, from the Netherlands against one of Uzbekistan's young female talents

Right: Jan

Paul from the Netherlands plays with the black pieces.

Peter against the Uzbek U10 champion

And so our first test at the boards awaited us: a team match against a selection of young Uzbek players. In the end, we won a closely contested match 15-12 - and came away with one clear lesson: it is better not to underestimate Uzbek talent.

Carpet dealer playing chess

Samarkand - culture in the morning, chess in the afternoon

The next morning, we travelled by bus to Samarkand. The name alone conjures up images. Of caravans, silk and tales from the Arabian Nights. And some of that quickly became reality: at Siyob Bazaar, the air was filled with the scent of spices, piles of nuts and fruit rose from the stalls - and there were the famous round Samarkand flatbreads with their intricate patterns.

The national dish, plov, is served here

A flatbread with the typical bread stamp

And then there was Registan! You know the square from pictures. But it only reveals its full impact when you are standing yourself between the three monumental madrasas, the historic elite centres of learning.

Registan with its three madrasas

The travel group

A laser show in the evening

Laser show at Registan

Our days in Samarkand soon settled into a pleasant rhythm: culture in the morning, chess in the afternoon. Then we headed out to the Olympiad at the Expo venue. A day ticket cost 20 dollars - and gave us the wonderful opportunity to watch the world's elite from close range.

Chess faces

In its own way, the huge playing hall was no less impressive than Registan. Hundreds of players, professionals and amateurs from more than 200 countries - the Olympiad gives them all a face. We experienced that peculiar mixture of absolute silence at the boards and international chatter outside the playing hall, and suddenly we were no longer watching a livestream from home as we had just a few days earlier, but right in the middle of it all.

Tashkent - a trip underground

Even before the final round, it was time to say goodbye to Samarkand. We continued by train to Tashkent - and into a very different Uzbek reality.

After the devastating earthquake of 1966, large parts of the capital were rebuilt. Wide streets, spacious squares, monumental buildings and plenty of greenery characterise the city.

One of its attractions, however, lies underground. So we took the metro. What elsewhere is simply public transport is also a small architectural tour in Tashkent. Kosmonavtlar station particularly stayed in our memories - an underground homage to Soviet space travel and its cosmonauts.

Back above ground, we stopped by the famous Hotel Uzbekistan. We did not content ourselves with its striking façade, but simply walked into its grand lobby as well.

Of all pairings, Germany against the Netherlands

On Sunday afternoon, however, Tashkent passed by outside the bus windows somewhat unnoticed for a while. Inside, our attention was focused elsewhere.

Almost everyone was staring at their phones.

The final round of the Olympiad was under way in Samarkand. And as if someone making the pairings had thought specifically of our travel group, one of the decisive matches was: Germany against the Netherlands.

For the German side, bronze was at stake. Matthias Bluebaum defeated Jorden van Foreest. And when Frederik Svane and Loek van Wely shook hands agreeing a draw at around half past five, it was confirmed: Germany had won bronze!

So the five Germans had a little more reason to celebrate that afternoon than the nine Dutch. Never mind. We were still sitting on the same bus, travelling together through Tashkent, and had long since discovered that both sides got along perfectly well even when, for once, more than honour was at stake in a chess match.

Four out of four - and a medal for zero out of zero

On Monday, it was our turn again.

At the Olympic Museum, we faced a young Uzbek team for the second time. Once again, we managed to win, but only one player had a perfect record after both matches: Yuri! Four points from four games, one hundred per cent.

That earned him a trophy - imposing, heavy and ideally suited to forcing a fresh calculation of the permitted luggage allowance for the journey home.

The awards ceremony

The trophy did contain one small inaccuracy, however: in gold lettering, the match was immortalised as "Uzbekistan - Netherlands". The rest of us Europeans from Germany and Italy took it in good humour.

And then there was still a bronze medal to award. Several players were tied for third place in the individual standings, but there was only one medal.

What to do? Ardjan found a Solomonic solution - and presented it to Monika.

She was the only non-chess player in our group. For eight days, she had endured opening variations, game analyses, results and probably more chess conversations than anyone without a personal interest in 64 squares could reasonably be expected to tolerate. The good spirit of our group received the medal.

Perhaps it was the nicest awards ceremony of the entire trip.

The chess world - a place for good people

At the farewell dinner that followed at Café Olympia, the wonderful Uzbek cuisine was served once again.

And there was a surprise cake, because one member of the group had a very personal reason to celebrate that evening: Michael turned 60! By then, at the latest, it became clear how quickly time can pass, how quickly eight days can go by. And sometimes it is only on the journey home that you realise how much of a trip actually stays with you.

A birthday surprise

John was almost home again when he wrote to the group: "The laughter, the stimulating conversations, the constant sense of wonder and the boundless freedom made this trip an unforgettable experience".

Yuri felt similarly: "Perhaps we will see each other again one day. After all, the chess world is not so large; it is a place for good people".

Fifteen people had spent eight days together in Bukhara, Samarkand and Tashkent. The fact that everything fitted together so wonderfully was due in no small part to Ardjan. He had combined culture and chess perfectly. Much could be planned and organised. What grew out of it could not.

In the end, there was certainly no trace of the much-cited German-Dutch rivalry. Instead, something else had genuinely emerged.

Something that needs no grand concluding statement. One from an old film will do. In Casablanca , Humphrey Bogart says: "I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship".

A line that could just as well have been spoken in Bukhara, Samarkand or Tashkent.

title: Birthday Boy Wesley So Starts U.S. Championship With Topsy-Turvy Win
summary: Three-time national champion GM Wesley So celebrated his 33rd birthday with a win over GM Sam Shankland in the first round of the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship, which started in St. Louis on Friday. GMs Jeffery Xiong and Awonder Liang also started with a win, scoring over GMs Sam Sevian and Hans Niemann, respectively. The 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship saw four decisive games in the first round, among them an unfortunate queen drop by GM Irina Krush in a clearly better position that enabled WIM Rachael Li to win. IM Anna Zatonskih and FMs Thalia Cervantes and Megan Paragua were the others to start the event with a win. The second round of both the tournaments will be on Saturday, October 10, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. And just like that, the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship and U.S. Women’s Chess Championship are underway! Dr. Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield rang the bell to officially kick off Round 1 at the Saint Louis Chess Club. 🔔 The games are on, and two weeks of exciting chess lie ahead. Let’s go! #USChessChamps Standings After Round 1: Open Standings After Round 1: Women Round 1 Results: Open The prize fund for the tournament stays identical to last year at a base of $250,000. But the tournament features bonus prizes for finishing first outright, a number of wins in a row, and a strong finish. The tournament is also an official tournament for the U.S. FIDE zone, serving as the qualification event for the next World Cup. The only change to the lineup from the previous year's championship is that Xiong replaces GM Dariusz Swiercz. After the games between GMs Levon Aronian and Fabiano Caruana, and GMs Abhimanyu Mishra and Ray Robson ended in draws without incident, Liang scored the first win of the day against Niemann. Surprisingly, Liang himself was not too impressed by his win when he spoke after the game. "It was a pretty bad game overall, the worst game of both sections... We both were missing everything." It was a pretty bad game overall, the worst game of both sections. —Awonder Liang Of course, the game did feature a number of tiny mistakes by both players, the biggest being Liang's missed opportunity to win Niemann's queen.

title: Wesley So, Awonder Liang Lead Open; Paragua, Cervantes Lead Women With Perfect Scores
summary: GMs Wesley So and Awonder Liang won again in round two of the 2026 U.S. Chess Championship to lead with 2/2 perfect scores. So was much worse against GM Jeffery Xiong but turned it around, while Liang converted an endgame to give GM Sam Sevian his second loss. We saw a first win by GM Fabiano Caruana against his second, GM Grigoriy Oparin, in the last game to end after 73 moves. Caruana is now the only player a half-point behind the leaders. The bottom two seeds of the 2026 U.S. Women's Chess Championship lead with perfect scores after two rounds. FM Megan Paragua found a stylish queen sacrifice to finish off IM Carissa Yip, while WGM Thalia Cervantes played a crushing counter-exchange sacrifice to defeat WIM Rachael Li. IM Anna Sargsyan blundered a pawn in the opening against IM Tatev Abrahamyan but ended up winning the game, as did IM Alice Lee against WGM Jennifer Yu. GM Irina Krush bounced back from Friday's queen blunder with a fierce attack against IM Rose Atwell. IM Nazi Paikidze vs. IM Anna Zatonskih was the only draw of the round. The third round of both tournaments will be on Sunday, October 11, starting at 1 p.m. ET / 19:00 CEST / 10:30 p.m. IST. Standings After Round 2: Open Standings After Round 2: Women Half the games were decisive, and the number of co-leaders shrank from three to two. Round 2 Results: Open Of the three draws, an Exchange Slav in GM Andy Woodward vs. GM Abhimanyu Mishra was the most solid game (99 accuracy by both). GM Sam Shankland played an early 9.Ng5 against GM Ray Robson, borrowing an idea from GM Matthias Bluebaum vs. GM Anish Giri in the 2026 FIDE Candidates Tournament, but the complicated game nevertheless simmered down. GM Levon Aronian played the Jaenisch Gambit with the black pieces against GM Hans Niemann, but neither side made any serious mistake—on the board, that is. The game had a funny ending, however, as Aronian made an incorrect draw claim in a dead-equal position, laughed as the game continued, only for Niemann to claim the draw (correctly) a few moves later. Levon Aronian seemingly makes an incorrect draw claim, only for the game to end a few moves later with Hans Niemann claiming the draw! https://t.co/UxO8T04A54 https://t.co/u79R8vxlth Liang was the first to win, from the black side of a King's Indian Attack. He explained the importance of the early move order: "I think Sam probably confused himself a little bit in the opening and just got a very bad position almost immediately... it was probably fine for him for a long time and then all of a sudden I was winning, and he had no defense." Indeed, Black was varying degrees of "better" throughout the game—usually only slightly—but the slow 32.Kg2?? lost the game on the spot. Liang found an entertaining way to convert his advantage, first sacrificing his knight and then his rook to pave the way for the connected passed pawns.
